summary: Baldwin Park sits in the San Gabriel Valley, roughly 20 miles east of downtown Los Angeles, on the flat, alluvial plain beneath the San Gabriel Mountains — and one of the first things that jumps out about this 6.8-square-mile city is its density: over 10,000 people per square mile, which is tighter than many neighborhoods inside L.A. proper, yet the streetscape reads as modest single-family homes and small apartment buildings rather than towers. The I-10 and I-210 freeways bracket the city, making it a textbook commuter node for the warehousing and logistics corridor that stretches east through the Inland Empire, as well as for healthcare and public-sector jobs scattered across the SGV. With a median home price around $588,000 against a median household income near $79,000, the price-to-income ratio lands above seven — steep enough that purchasing typically demands either substantial savings or dual incomes, while the median rent of roughly $1,800 consumes about 28 percent of that same median income. Year-round sunshine averaging over nine hours a day and a mean high near 78°F keep the climate mild, though summer heat in this inland valley pushes well past that average. Motor vehicle theft runs notably high at nearly 490 per 100,000, a pattern consistent with freeway-adjacent San Gabriel Valley cities. Baldwin Park is, at its core, an extraordinarily compressed commuter city where the math of homeownership requires more income than the local economy typically generates.
